client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away from cancer last year. I keep trying to throw myself into work, but I just can't focus — I'll be in the middle of something and suddenly I'm just... gone, thinking about her, and nothing gets done. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because it's not like anything you say is going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom and then trying to push through the grief by staying busy, only to find the grief finds you anyway. You're right that nothing can bring her back, and I want you to know I'm not here to fix that or minimize it, but sometimes just having a space to say what's true out loud can shift something small inside. I'm curious — when those moments hit you at work and you're suddenly "gone," what kinds of things tend to come up for you in those thoughts about her?

client: It's usually just... random stuff, honestly. Like I'll see someone eating a sandwich at their desk and suddenly I'm thinking about how she used to make these terrible egg salad sandwiches that I always complained about, and now I'd give anything to eat one. And then I just feel this wave of guilt, like I wasted so much time being annoyed by small things instead of just being grateful she was there.
therapist: Those little unexpected moments — a sandwich, a smell, a song — can carry so much grief, and what you're describing sounds like a very tender kind of love showing up in disguise. That guilt you feel makes a lot of sense, but I want to gently offer this: complaining about egg salad sandwiches is just what it looks like to be a normal person living alongside someone you assumed would always be there — it wasn't a failure of love, it was just life. What do you think your mom would say if she heard you beating yourself up over this?

client: I want to believe that, I really do. But my mom was the kind of person who would probably laugh and say something like "oh, stop being so dramatic" — and somehow that makes it worse, not better, because then I just feel stupid for still carrying this around years later. Like even in my imagination she's kind of dismissing me, which... I don't know, maybe that says something I'm not ready to look at yet.
therapist: That moment of insight at the end — "maybe that says something I'm not ready to look at yet" — shows a lot of courage, and I don't want to rush past it. It sounds like there's something quietly painful in the idea that even her imagined voice doesn't fully make room for your grief, and I wonder if that's a dynamic that felt familiar even when she was alive — like your sadness sometimes didn't quite get to land anywhere safe with her. Does that resonate at all, or does it feel off?

client: Yeah... it resonates more than I want it to. I think there was always this unspoken thing where I had to be okay around her, like my falling apart would have been too much for her to handle, so I just... didn't. And now she's gone and I still can't figure out where to put all of it, because even in my head she's still kind of unavailable for the hard stuff.
therapist: What you just named is really significant — you spent years learning to fold yourself smaller emotionally to protect her, and now you're left holding all that unexpressed grief with no clear place for it to go, even internally. That's an exhausting and lonely way to have loved someone, and it makes so much sense that you're struggling to process this, because in some ways you never fully had permission to fall apart *with* her. I'm wondering — now that you can see that pattern a little more clearly, what do you think you actually needed back then that you didn't let yourself have?

client: I think what I needed was just... to be able to say "I'm scared too" without worrying it would make things worse for her. Like, I needed someone to hold space for both of us, not just me holding space for her while pretending I was fine. But even saying that out loud now feels almost selfish, like I'm somehow betraying her memory by admitting she couldn't give me that.
therapist: Saying that out loud isn't a betrayal — it's actually one of the most honest acts of love, because it means you're finally seeing her as a whole, imperfect person rather than protecting an idealized version of her at your own expense. Acknowledging that she had limitations doesn't erase how much you loved her or how much she loved you; both things can be true at once. I'm curious — what does it feel like in your body right now, having actually said that out loud, maybe for the first time?

client: It feels like there's this tight knot in my chest that loosened just a little, but also like I'm waiting for something bad to happen because I said it. Like some part of me still expects to be punished for admitting she wasn't perfect. I don't know if that makes sense, but it's almost scarier to feel the relief than to feel the guilt.
therapist: It makes complete sense — that loosening in your chest is real, and so is the fear around it, because relief can feel dangerous when you've spent so long believing that holding it all together was how you kept things safe. That waiting-for-punishment feeling is worth paying attention to, because it tells us there's a belief somewhere underneath all this that says your needs or your honesty come with a cost. I'm wondering — where do you think you first learned that telling the truth about how you felt was something to be afraid of?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... it was probably at home, growing up. My mom had a lot going on, and whenever I tried to say I was scared or upset about something, it always seemed to make things worse for her, so I just learned to keep it quiet and act like everything was fine.
therapist: What you just described is a child doing something incredibly adaptive — learning to shrink their own emotional needs to keep the peace — and that little version of you was doing the best they could with what they had. But that same strategy that protected you then is still running now, making it hard to let yourself be held, even by your own grief. I'm curious — as you sit with that image of your younger self learning to go quiet, what do you feel toward them?

client: I feel... sad for them, I guess. Like, I want to tell that kid that they didn't have to do that, that it wasn't their job to manage everyone else's feelings. But then there's also this weird guilt, like even feeling sad about it feels self-indulgent somehow, like I'm making myself the victim of something that wasn't even that bad.
therapist: The compassion you just offered that child is real and it's right — and I want to gently point out that you did it, even if just for a moment, which means some part of you already knows they deserved more than they got. That voice calling it "self-indulgent" is worth examining, because it sounds a lot like the same voice that told you to stay quiet back then — it's not an objective truth, it's an old rule you learned to survive. What would you say to a close friend who told you the same story you just told me — would you call *their* sadness self-indulgent?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably want to sit with them and tell them it made sense that they felt that way. But it's different when it's me — I don't know why, it just feels different, like I don't get the same... allowance, I guess.
therapist: That word — "allowance" — is really telling, because it suggests that somewhere along the way you internalized the idea that compassion is something you have to earn or be granted, rather than something you simply deserve as a human being. And yet you'd give it freely to a friend without a second thought, which means you *have* the capacity for it — the only thing standing in the way is this old belief that you're somehow the exception. What do you think it would take, even in some small way, to start treating yourself as someone who gets the same allowance you'd give everyone else?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it logically — like, yes, that makes sense on paper. But when I try to actually apply it to myself, there's this immediate wall that goes up, like my brain just goes "yeah, but that's different, you actually messed up." I think what it would take is... I honestly don't know, because every time I try to be kind to myself about the situation with my friend, it just feels like I'm making excuses for something I genuinely did wrong.
therapist: That wall your brain puts up — "yeah, but that's different, you actually messed up" — is really important information, because it sounds like there's a specific situation with a friend underneath all of this that's carrying a lot of weight for you. There's a meaningful difference between taking honest responsibility for something and using it as evidence that you fundamentally don't deserve kindness — and I wonder if your brain might be doing the latter. Would you feel comfortable telling me a little about what happened with your friend, so we can look at it together rather than letting it sit as this unnamed thing you're judging yourself against?
